In short

  • The problem: robot models are trusted before anyone checks that they move the way they claim; modeling errors stay silent until hardware.
  • Who has it: university rover teams, ROS 2 hobbyists and small startups, with no test team and no test budget.
  • Why a gate: no free tool gives a pass/fail verdict with evidence.

Research brief · Compiled October 25–26, 2026 · America/Los_Angeles · For the RobotForge scope lock

A robot model should have to pass before anyone trusts it.

RobotForge is a proposed open-source acceptance gate for robot models: a model has to pass a measured driving test in simulation before anyone trusts it, and the verdict comes with evidence (how the test works). This brief documents whether the problem is real, who already solves pieces of it, and what to build first. Short answer: the problem is documented by the field's own research, and the verdict-shaped hole in the tooling is still empty.

The gate, step by step

  1. 1Describe a wheeled robot — links, joints, wheels, sensors.
  2. 2Generate its URDF/SDF model files.
  3. 3Spawn it headless in Gazebo — no GUI, no display, CI-friendly.
  4. 4Drive fixed maneuvers — straight ~1 m, turn in place ~90°.
  5. 5Compare reported odometry against simulator ground truth.
  6. 6Stamp a verdict — PASS or FAIL, with the measured evidence attached.

Built for university rover teams, ROS 2 hobbyists, and small robotics startups — the teams with no platform group and no test infrastructure budget.

Afzal et al. 2020
2025

AWS RoboMaker — the one cloud service offering pass/fail sim metrics at scale — was discontinued on 10 September 2025.

The Robot Report, 2025-09-10
Verdict: build it

No tool found produces a pass/fail verdict with evidence, for a small team, headlessly, for free. Static validators never run the robot. Gazebo ships syntax checks and a GUI inertia viewer, not a verdict. Nav2's system tests serve Nav2's maintainers. Isaac Sim's minimum spec — an RTX 4080 with 16 GB VRAM — excludes most student laptops and free CI runners. The one commercial verdict product, AWS RoboMaker, no longer exists.

One honesty constraint, carried through this whole brief: Gazebo physics is not bit-reproducible, so the claim is never "deterministic." It is pass/fail within stated tolerances over a fixed, seeded scenario — with repeatability reported, not assumed.

Evidence tags used throughout: Read live the source page was opened and read during this research. Via index the claim rests on search-index / search-result text. Anything weaker is flagged in place, and §8 lists everything that could not be verified.

01

The pain is documented — by the field itself

The strongest evidence isn't forum complaints. It's a peer-reviewed-style survey of 82 robotics developers — Afzal, Katz, Le Goues & Timperley, "A Study on the Challenges of Using Robotics Simulators for Testing" (2020) — plus the ROS ecosystem's own quality-assurance reporting. Their findings read like a requirements document for this tool.

"Most simulations are NOT designed to run headless, nor are they easily scriptable for automatic invocation." — Survey respondent P34, in Afzal et al. 2020 Via index
  • Headless is the exception, not the default. Participants preferred headless execution for automation and named its absence a major difficulty. One respondent (P37) had to connect a physical display to a Jenkins CI server to run simulation properly; another (P24): "no obvious test harnesses available for the simulation environments I use."
  • CI deployment is a named failure point. Respondents reported simulators difficult to deploy in CI/cloud (P62), being unable to set up a CI pipeline on GPU machines (P66), and cloud GPU VMs being expensive (P77). Gazebo's own documentation now concedes that "setting up a Gazebo environment in a Continuous Integration (CI) pipeline can often be a complex and time-consuming task" — and ships a setup-gazebo GitHub Action to mitigate it. Gazebo CI docsVia index
  • Resets aren't repeatable. P7: "Resetting gazebo simulations was not repeatable enough to get good data." The survey's conclusion about the de facto ROS simulator is blunt: Gazebo "does not adequately support headless execution, lacks reproducibility, and performs poorly" on complex environments.
  • The GPU-sensor path was historically blocked. Headless runs once required an OpenGL X server; Gazebo's headless-rendering documentation calls the workaround steps "complex and error prone" and documents the EGL-based --headless-rendering path (OGRE2 only). The same doc notes running simulation on a remote computer is "often desirable." Headless rendering docsVia index
  • ROS QA is inconsistent at the process level. The ROSIN / ROS-Industrial quality-assurance report found QA practices inconsistent across the ROS community, no QA ownership, and roughly 1 in 5 ROS bugs detected at runtime — often by end users — where a CI service was expected to catch many errors earlier. ROSIN D3.1 reportVia index
  • Reproducibility is still an open research problem. A 2026 paper on deterministic ROS 2 execution (RSLCPP) notes ROS 2's asynchronous multiprocess design complicates reproducibility across hardware, "complicating benchmarking and CI." arXiv 2601.07052Via index

Design consequence, stated up front: because bit-exact determinism isn't on offer, the gate reports spread — run each maneuver k times and publish the distribution — instead of pretending one run is proof. See §7, item 8.

02

Modeling errors are silent, and found late

URDFs are written by hand, checked by tools that only verify the file parses, and converted to SDF by a pipeline that can drop parts of the model without a word. The failures surface later — as a robot that shakes, explodes, or quietly drives wrong.

"Making URDF files is a tremendous pain as the only good way to do it right now is by hand which is faulty and error prone." — Survey respondent P4, in Afzal et al. 2020 Via index

The official checker stops at syntax

check_urdf validates structure, not physics

The official ROS tool parses a URDF and prints the kinematic chain or an error. Tesseract's documentation summarizes that it "catches XML errors and basic structural issues" — while collision-mesh quality, misaligned frames, joint limits, and self-collision still require visual inspection. Gazebo's own command, gz sdf -k, is likewise syntax validation only. Neither executes physics or compares behavior.

Tesseract URDF docs · gz man pageVia index

A physics-aware validator states the gap

"Can still silently fail in any physics-based simulator"

The PyPI package urdf-validator (a vendor claim, but it matches the check_urdf documentation): "A URDF that passes check_urdf can still silently fail in any physics-based simulator — collapsing robots, undersized motors, unstable configurations." Its worked examples are real upstream defects: Fetch gripper-finger links with non-positive-definite inertia (eigenvalue 0.0) and PR2 links missing inertial blocks entirely.

It is the closest static prior art — and it never starts Gazebo, drives the robot, or compares odometry to ground truth. A complement, not a competitor. See §5.Via index

Vendor data, wrong for years

Universal Robots shipped UR5e masses copied from the UR5

The official ROS 2 description for the UR5e carried link masses "copied from UR5 CB3." Nobody's tooling caught it — a user checked by hand and filed an issue; the maintainer agreed the reporter was "absolutely correct." Fixed via PR #187; the issue closed 2024-09-06. Cited here as pain evidence — a closed issue, not an open need.

Universal_Robots_ROS2_Description #186Read live

Conversion drops parts silently

An IMU extension vanished — "without any warning message"

sdformat issue #1372: a <gazebo> IMU extension whose reference string didn't match a real link was "completely ignored, without any warning message or error" during URDF→SDF conversion. The maintainer's reply: "Ouch! That's a tough one to debug. +1 for a warning message if an extension references an unknown link." Still open. The gate's structural tier exists to make exactly this class of drop an explicit failure.

sdformat #1372Read live

Why robots "explode" in Gazebo

Wrong inertia is the classic cause. A ROS Answers thread attributes Gazebo shaking to "bad inertia matrices, bad physics settings, joint problems," with debugging described as a process of elimination, parameter by parameter. A community wiki's list of "exploding robot" causes: PID gains, inertia values too small, collision overlaps, joints starting outside limits, solver instability. A beginner-facing differential-drive tutorial states it plainly: "Robot vibrates or explodes in Gazebo: inertia values are wrong… No value should be 0.0 or below 1e-6" — and warns wheels render sideways if the cylinder joint axis isn't rotated (rpy="${pi/2} 0 0").Via index

A simulation textbook chapter frames the deeper version: "a robot description good enough for visualization is not automatically good enough for contact-rich control" — a missing <inertial> block can yield high simulation success and near-zero hardware success while compiling without any error. Its audit checklist covers units, mesh scale, inertias, joint axes, damping, limits, and collision shapes.Via index

The inertia rules themselves are well specified — the matrix must be symmetric positive-definite and satisfy the triangle inequalities (ixx + iyy ≥ izz, etc.), and every link needs physically plausible mass, center of mass, and inertia. What's missing is any tool that enforces them automatically. Gazebo inertia tutorialVia index

03

Odometry is not ground truth — and users keep rediscovering it

The conceptual core of the gate — comparing what the robot reports against what actually happened — is a live, open source of confusion inside Gazebo itself. Two open gz-sim bugs are users hand-building exactly the comparison RobotForge automates.

DiffDrive odometry "is not ground truth… it simulates how odometry would be calculated from the model's kinematics and joint state." Ground truth comes from a different system: OdometryPublisher. — Gazebo maintainer, in gz-sim #872 Read live
  • gz-sim #872 (open since 2021-06-21, labeled bug and help wanted): a robot spawned at (2, 2) reported odometry starting at (0, …). The reporter asked for clearer semantics; the maintainer's clarification above is the distinction the gate productizes — DiffDrive odometry is the device under test, OdometryPublisher is the reference. Read the issue
  • gz-sim #2862 (open, labeled bug, filed 2025-04-15): odometry found "delayed or stale… usually behind robots actual position" — discovered by a user running an "exhaustive test of the diff drive system" to simulate an EKF filter node. That hand-built test is a ready-made regression scenario for the gate. Read the issue
  • The maneuvers are classical, not invented. UMBmark (Borenstein & Feng, 1996) — the standard systematic-odometry-error method — uses straight runs and 90° spot turns precisely because they expose the two dominant systematic errors: unequal effective wheel diameters (Ed) and uncertain effective wheelbase (Eb). The gate's two tests are that method, miniaturized. UMBmark paper (PDF)Via index

Try the arithmetic the gate automates

From a wheeled-robot odometry guide's worked example: a nominal wheel radius of 33.0 mm against an actual 32.5 mm (tire compression) is a 1.5% distance error — 15 cm over 10 m — and wheel slip is undetectable from encoders alone. Drag the sliders and watch a sub-millimeter modeling error become a failed run.Via index

Model declares 33.0 mm. Tire compression, wear, and manufacturing tolerance move the real value.
The gate's test runs ~1 m; longer runs just scale the same percentage error.
UMBmark's Eb: the turn test's target. Real configs ship empirical corrections — PAL Robotics' PMB-2 uses multiplier parameters; a TurtleBot4 config carries wheel_separation_multiplier: 1.06793648481 (snippet-level evidence).
Ground truth travels10.00 m
Odometry reports10.15 m
Distance error+15.4 cm · +1.54%
Commanded turn90.0°
Odometry reports turn of92.3°
Heading error+2.25°
Gate verdict: FAIL

Illustrative arithmetic, not measured data: odometry integrates wheel rotation using the declared radius, so reported distance scales by 33.0 ÷ actual radius; reported rotation scales by (1 + wheelbase error). Verdict uses an example tolerance of ±2% distance / ±2° heading. The point stands at any tolerance: the error is in the model, it's systematic, and nothing in the current toolchain measures it for you.

The same numbers live in two files that must agree

Wheel radius and separation appear in the URDF geometry, again in the DiffDrive plugin's SDF tags (<wheel_separation>, <wheel_radius>, <left_joint>, <right_joint>), and again in the ros2_control controller YAML. Project documentation warns that URDF-vs-YAML disagreement produces odometry error or controller startup failure — a cross-file consistency hazard no single-file linter catches. Vendors confirm real robots never match CAD: PAL Robotics' PMB-2 calibration docs cite wheel diameter tolerances of ±1–2 mm, tire wear, assembly tolerances, tire pressure, and floor interaction, corrected with empirically determined multipliers.Via index

Scope honesty: a gate comparing odometry to simulator ground truth catches model self-inconsistency — wrong radius, separation, or axes in the description versus what the simulated physics does. It does not close the sim-to-real gap, and the pitch shouldn't claim it does.

04

The audience under-tests — that's the survey's headline

The primary audience source is Snider et al., "University Rover Challenge: Tutorials and Team Survey" — a book chapter surveying URC teams — plus current competition reporting. URC draws hundreds of students across 80+ teams (in 2017: 35 rovers, 500+ students) who spend a year building a rover from scratch under a $15,000 spending cap, which makes ROS's free ecosystem "a natural fit… to cut costs." This is precisely the segment that cannot buy test infrastructure.Via index

"Teams most often expressed difficulty using IMUs or not testing their rover enough." — Snider et al., URC team survey Via index
  • The winning teams' advice is "test more, earlier, with everything." Of 2nd-place Team Continuum: asked what they wished they had done differently, "the answer was always the same: more field tests with all components of the rover" — advice the chapter notes is "often given by other teams." Field testing forces the team to finish sooner, but it demands the whole team organized and present with the finished rover. Today, that expensive in-person route is the only route to the feedback.
  • Odometry failing at competition is documented. Team R3 (Ryerson): "As a result of wheel slippage on sand, Team R3 did not use wheel odometry… because our IMU was not working well enough to produce a good fused result, at the competition we did not actually use the ekf localization ROS nodes" — they fell back to visual odometry only. Another surveyed team "had plans to use MoveIt but due to lack of testing time used velocity control… at competition."
  • Current practice is a human watching a GUI. The University of Michigan MRover team's autonomy starter project instructs new members to open Gazebo and a visualizer, run the navigation node, and "Watch it move to (5.5, 2)… see the tag, and finally reach the tag" — pass/fail is eyeballs, with no automated verdict and no recorded evidence. (Wiki-mirror source; indicative.) MRover starter projectVia index
  • It is still happening in 2026. Michigan's MRover finished 3rd at CIRC and 5th at URC 2026 after "a summer filled with troubleshooting and continued testing" — and its write-up documents competition features, built for the new Heist mission, where "many of the tasks the rover had to perform had not yet been tested ahead of the competition" and the team "did not have enough time to fully test and get this feature working before the competition." (The same write-up's forfeits were hardware — a Jetson that failed to reboot, traced to a bad PCIe card, and damaged wiring. Relevant to under-testing generally; not model-validation failures.) MRover CIRC 2026 write-upVia index
  • The robots are real field machines. CIRC's 2026 rules specify a single self-contained rover, a <50 kg target, a 0.8 m door constraint, ≥1 h per task, and operation in rain, mud, snow, and darkness — outdoor robots whose testing today is physical by default. CIRC 2026 rulesVia index

Claim to keep honest: "the robot is in the lab and the team is remote"

This is the founding story for a headless, run-it-from-home gate — and this research did not find a source that directly documents it. No team write-up or forum thread located states that members cannot test because the robot sits in a lab/shop while they are remote. The demand is supported only indirectly: developers want headless, scriptable, CI-deployable simulation (Afzal et al.); one needed a physical display attached to a CI server; Gazebo's docs call remote/cloud execution "often desirable"; URC teams are budget-capped and under-test.

Until a team states it directly, present the remote-testing story as a hypothesis consistent with the survey data — not as a documented fact. Same discipline for competition failures: none found was traced specifically to an unvalidated URDF or odometry parameter error. See §8.

05

Prior art: every neighbor is one layer away

The headline question — does anything already produce a pass/fail verdict with evidence, for a small team, headlessly, for free? — answers no. Each tool below covers a slice. Static validators sit below the gate (no execution), Nav2's tests beside it (wrong scope), Isaac Sim above it (a platform, GPU-gated), and RoboMaker is gone.

ToolWhat it doesHeadlessFreeRuns the robotVerdict + evidence
check_urdf Parses URDF; prints kinematic chain or parse error Yes Yes No Parse only; no physics checks
gz sdf -k Validates SDF syntax Yes Yes No Syntax only
Gazebo GUI inertia view Visual per-link inertia boxes vs. bounding box No — manual GUI procedure Yes Spawn only No — human eyeballing
urdf-validator Physics-aware static URDF checks: schema, positive-definite inertia, COM, gravity-torque margins, support-polygon stability; CI exit codes; optional MuJoCo cross-check Yes Yes No — static only Static verdicts only — no driving, no odometry-vs-truth
yourdfpy Python URDF load / validate / visualize, forward kinematics Yes Yes No Validation errors; no behavior verdict
launch_testing (ROS 2) Framework: launch nodes (e.g. Gazebo + Nav2), run unittest assertions, XUnit output Yes Yes If you build the test Framework only — no prebuilt model acceptance test; docs warn tests are "more complex both to set up and to run"
Nav2 system tests Gazebo-based navigation system tests used in Nav2 CI Yes Yes Yes Yes, for Nav2 behavior — but Nav2-stack-specific, heavyweight, "primarily for use in Nav2 CI" by its maintainers
NVIDIA Isaac Sim Full GPU simulation platform: PhysX, RTX sensors, synthetic data, ROS 2 bridge, URDF import Yes Free download (license terms apply) Yes No built-in small-team acceptance verdict. Minimum spec: RTX 4080, 16 GB VRAM, 32 GB RAM, 50 GB SSD; "GPUs without RT Cores (A100, H100) are not supported"
AWS RoboMaker Cloud simulation at scale via Gazebo, with pass/fail metrics Yes (cloud) Discontinued 2025-09-10 Yes Was yes — the product no longer exists. Post-mortem: target users needed "just a few" simulations, not thousands — consistent with an unmet small-scale need (that inference is ours, not the article's)
Foxglove "One workspace to debug robot behavior, live or recorded" — time-synchronized multimodal inspection, teleop panels n/a Freemium No No — observability, not execution or verdicts. A plausible evidence-report viewer, not a competitor
Rerun SDK logging + viewer for multimodal robot data n/a Open-source core No No — visualization/logging
InOrbit / Formant RobOps: fleet operations, teleoperation, incident management for deployed robots n/a Commercial No No — operations on real fleets, not pre-deployment model gates
The Construct Cloud ROS learning environment; browser-based sim for courses Browser Freemium / courses Yes, for learning No acceptance-verdict product (characterization from site material at search level — light-touch)

Beyond syntax validation and the GUI inertia procedure, Gazebo itself ships headless server mode with the EGL --headless-rendering option for GPU sensors, and CI packaging via the setup-gazebo GitHub Action — the sanctioned building blocks for the gate's harness. No shipped "run maneuvers and grade the model" tool appears in the documentation reviewed.Via index

07

The build list, ranked by evidence

Eight candidate tests for a 10-day MVP, ranked by strength of documented evidence × cheapness to implement in a headless Gazebo harness × directness of fit to the odometry-vs-ground-truth concept. Each item names the evidence it answers.

  1. 1

    Structural URDF/SDF sanity

    File parses (check_urdf + gz sdf -k); joint/link references resolve; no kinematic loops or duplicate names; mesh files exist; and — the differentiator — every <gazebo> extension reference resolves to a real link, via a post-conversion diff of declared vs. actually-present sensors and plugins.

    Evidence: sdformat #1372 (extension "completely ignored, without any warning") · check_urdf's documented limits · Afzal P4 on hand-authored URDF pain.

  2. 2

    Mass / inertia plausibility

    Every non-fixed link has mass > 0 and an <inertial>; inertia is symmetric positive-definite; triangle inequalities hold; center of mass sits within link geometry / support region; total mass compared against a user-declared expectation.

    Evidence: Gazebo inertia tutorial (rules; rotated inertia "happens often") · UR5e wrong vendor masses (#186) · Fetch/PR2 defects in urdf-validator's examples · shaking/exploding-robot threads.

  3. 3

    Cross-file consistency — wheel parameters

    Wheel radius, wheel separation, wheel joint names, and joint axis direction agree across URDF geometry, DiffDrive plugin / SDF tags, and controller YAML.

    Evidence: URDF-vs-YAML mismatch → odometry error / startup failure · PMB-2 CAD-vs-real divergence and multiplier practice · DiffDrive plugin parameter surface.

  4. 4

    Spawn-stability check

    Spawn headless, step N seconds uncommanded. FAIL if the robot falls through the ground plane, tips, translates or rotates beyond a small threshold, or produces NaN / exploding joint states.

    Evidence: "Robot vibrates or explodes in Gazebo: inertia values are wrong" · exploding-robots cause list (inertia, collision overlap, joint limits, solver) · ROS Answers shaking-by-elimination debugging.

  5. 5

    Straight-line odometry test (~1 m)

    Command a straight drive; compare DiffDrive/controller odometry against OdometryPublisher ground truth: distance error %, lateral drift, heading drift. PASS within tolerance.

    Evidence: gz-sim #872 (odometry ≠ ground truth; maintainer clarification) · gz-sim #2862 (wrong/stale odometry, open bug) · wheel-radius error math (1.5% → 15 cm over 10 m) · UMBmark methodology.

  6. 6

    Turn-in-place heading test (~90°)

    Rotate in place; compare odometry yaw change against ground-truth yaw change; report heading error in degrees and %.

    Evidence: UMBmark — 90° spot turns expose uncertain effective wheelbase (Eb), one of the two dominant systematic errors · PMB-2 / TurtleBot4 separation-multiplier practice.

  7. 7

    Sensor / topic presence checks

    After spawn: odometry, joint_states, and each declared IMU/LiDAR/camera topic actually publishes at an expected rate; TF odom→base_link exists.

    Evidence: sdformat #1372 silent sensor drop · MRover-style manual topic/visual checking today · gz-sim #2668/#2803 ground-truth topic semantics.

  8. 8

    Square-path closure + repeatability reportStretch

    Run 4× (straight + 90° turn); report closure error. Repeat each maneuver k times and report the spread, not just the mean — repeatability reporting is itself the feature, given the field's reproducibility findings.

    Evidence: full UMBmark procedure (4×4 m square, 5 CW + 5 CCW), scaled down · Afzal reproducibility findings ("not repeatable enough to get good data").

Design constraints the evidence imposes

  • Ground truth from OdometryPublisher / PosePublisher; DiffDrive odometry is the device under test — per the maintainer semantics in #872. Document that OdometryPublisher pose is currently noise-free world pose (#2668), and resolve topics via the model namespace rather than hard-coding (#4104).
  • The evidence report is half the product. Per test it should carry: commanded maneuver, measured odometry value, ground-truth value, error, tolerance, verdict, and the model/config hashes. No tool in §5 provides this.
  • Ship the harness as a container / GitHub Action from day one. Gazebo's own CI doc calls setup "complex and time-consuming," and Afzal's respondents failed at exactly this step; the setup-gazebo action is the sanctioned building block.
  • Phrase determinism honestly: fixed scenario + stated tolerances + repeatability statistics (§1/§3) — never bit-exactness.
08

What this research could not verify

Open questions, stated plainly. Anything on this list should not appear in a pitch as established fact.

  1. ?

    "Teams can't test because the robot is in a lab while members are remote"

    No direct source found. Supported only indirectly (headless/CI demand in Afzal et al.; Gazebo's remote-execution rationale). Do not present as documented.

  2. ?

    A competition failure traced to an unvalidated URDF / odometry model error

    Not found. Documented competition failures were hardware (MRover PCIe/wiring, CIRC 2026) and real-robot sensing (Team R3 sand slip / IMU, URC survey). Related, but distinct.

  3. ?

    Nav2 system-tests documentation

    The docs page returned "Access Denied" when opened via the index; its characterization in §5 rests on the search-result snippet of that page.

  4. ?

    ros2_controllers #2251

    Title and date come from a live GitHub search listing only; the issue page was not individually opened.

  5. ?

    Isaac Sim requirements

    Read via the search-result text of NVIDIA's official requirements page (5.1.0), not a full page open; version-specific numbers will drift.

  6. ?

    TurtleBot4 wheel_separation_multiplier

    The value 1.06793648481 and its comment come via a DeepWiki summary of the configuration (snippet-level), not the raw config file.

  7. ?

    Formant and The Construct characterizations

    Light-touch, from vendor/roundup material at search level; neither was deep-read. Neither affects the §5 conclusion.

  8. ?

    LinkForge / fieldpilot-urdf

    Physics-linting claims seen in search results were not opened and are excluded from this brief entirely.

About this brief. Compiled October 25–26, 2026 (America/Los_Angeles) from primary sources where possible — project documentation, GitHub issues read live, a peer-reviewed-style survey, and competition team publications. "Read live" means the page was opened and read during the research; "Via index" means the claim rests on search-index text. Values are carried with the hedges their sources attach to them; §8 lists everything that could not be verified, including the remote-testing claim this project was founded on. Photos: University Rover Challenge field photo via franceszhu.space; DiffBot Gazebo screenshot from the ros-mobile-robots project.
